item.content:encoded:
The main joke is the tongue twisters, which I wrote myself and weren't in the book.

You and I differ on that point, then. The source material you're referencing is completely integral to the article, since you're literally containing something from a Dr. Seuss book and writing up their activities from said book in the logs. The reference is also apparently what people are responding to in the commentary and presumably the voting. I don't agree that the borrowing from Dr. Seuss is somehow a secondary element.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
The main joke is the tongue twisters, which I wrote myself and weren't in the book.
The goofy Seuss stuff and references are added on because the setup would be boring without them, an SCP-J that only makes one joke has to have a damn good joke to stand on, and because if I'm making the reference to Tweetle Beetles in the first place I may as well go all out with it.

That said, it's cool if you don't like it. Humour is subjective. I just think that the references are more of a secondary thing and that the primary thing would be a lot harder to make work without them, or at least that's how I was thinking about it while I wrote it.

item.content:encoded:
+ Click here to breach SCP-005-J-EX from containment.
- Click here to return SCP-005-J-EX to containment.

It's mostly based on the Doctor Seuss tongue twister/poem "Tweetle Beetle Battles" (or spelled "Tweedle Beetle Battles" if you'd prefer, though my copy of the book says "Tweetle" so I went with that). I guess that you could call Experiment Log 543-Sierra-Sigma-J that tongue twister on hard mode for a more mature older audience.
Then there are also other Seuss-y jokes/puns/references I put here and there to fill up the rest of the document.

The main joke is probably automatically lost on anyone who didn't read Fox in Socks, though I think the tongue twisters should still be enjoyable enough if you're into them.
